At the outset, allow me to extend my best wishes to you, the Bureau, and the Secretariat of the Third Committee for a fruitful and constructive term. Cyprus aligns with the statement delivered by the European Union, but allow me also to share the following in my national capacity. Mr. Chair, Cyprus considers human rights one of the cornerstones of the multilateral system and continues to place their promotion and protection at the heart of its foreign policy. As a member of the Human Rights Council for the 2025-2027 term, Cyprus remains firmly committed to contributing constructively to the Council's work and to advancing the universal promotion, protection, and fulfillment of human rights at both national and international levels. Mr. Chair, the people of Cyprus, which today proudly celebrates its 66th anniversary of independence, have experienced for the last 52 years gross violations of their human rights and fundamental freedoms as a result of the illegal Turkish military invasion and continued military occupation of one-third of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus in flagrant violation of international law and the UN Charter. More than one third of the population are still internally displaced, being denied the right to return and peacefully enjoy their properties. Instead, their land is subjected to unlawful exploitation by the occupation regime. Equally alarming is the occupying power's systemic policy of demographic engineering through the mass transfer of settlers, which constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law. The cultural and religious heritage of my country has also suffered irreparable loss, with over 500 churches looted, desecrated, or destroyed. The destruction of cultural heritage is recognized as a violation of international law and, under the Rome Statute, as a war crime. The few hundred enclaved Greek Cypriots and Maronites who remain in the occupied areas continue to face oppression and discrimination, including restrictions on education, religion, and access to their communities. At the same time, the fate of nearly half of the missing persons in Cyprus remains unresolved due to the refusal of Turkey to provide to the Committee of Missing Persons all relevant information from its military archives and grant unhindered access to what it classifies as military areas. In recounting the violations committed, it is equally important to acknowledge the restrictions suffered by the Turkish Cypriots living under occupation. Their freedom of expression, thought, religion and association are curtailed. Their daily lives are subjected to surveillance and interference, and their culture and identity are suppressed. The passage of time can never render human rights violations acceptable, nor can it weaken the obligation arising from international law. Cyprus will continue to firmly and consistently raise these violations in all relevant international fora until the rights and fundamental freedoms of all Cypriots are fully restored. Mr. Chair, around the world, women and girls continue to face discrimination, violence and persistent structural barriers. Cyprus remains firmly committed to advancing gender equality, eliminating all forms of discrimination, and promoting, protecting and fulfilling the rights of women and girls, including their full, equal and meaningful participation in all spheres of life. Preventing and eliminating violence against women and girls remains a key priority, alongside strengthening protection and support for victims and accountability for perpetrators. Cyprus is also addressing emerging forms of technology-facilitated gender-based violence through strengthened policy, institutional responses and multilateral cooperation, including through its participation in the High-Level Network of Gender-Responsive Policing. Mr. Chair, as we mark 20 years since the adoption of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Cyprus reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the full and equal enjoyment of human rights by persons with disabilities in accordance with the CRPD. We remain committed to advancing equality, accessibility, inclusion and independent living, while ensuring the meaningful participation of persons with disabilities in decisions that affect their lives. Through our National Strategy on Disability, Cyprus continues to strengthen its policies and support frameworks in close consultations with organizations of persons with disabilities. In this regard, Cyprus is honored to serve as Vice President of the Bureau of the 20th and 21st sessions of the Conference of States Parties of CRPD, representing the Asia-Pacific group. Cyprus is committed to upholding the rights of the child in accordance with the Convention on the Rights of the Child and its Optional Protocols, and constitutes one of our priorities as a member of the Human Rights Council. Through the National Strategy and Action Plan on Early Childhood Education and Care, targeted programs for children at risk, and support to families through child benefits, Cyprus promotes children's well-being, protection, and equal opportunities. Cyprus also supports children's meaningful participation in public life through initiatives such as the Cyprus Children's Parliament. Cyprus also strongly supports the full, effective and meaningful participation of young people in decision making at all levels, recognizing them as equal partners and key contributors to democratic, inclusive and sustainable societies. Cyprus continues to strengthen opportunities for young people to shape national policies and participate in decision making, while promoting youth empowerment through education, skills development, volunteering and creativity. We also support the work of the UN Youth Office in advancing meaningful youth engagement across the UN system and look forward to participating in the first UN Youth Town Hall. Mr. Chair, older persons are equally vital to society, contributing knowledge and experience, yet often face marginalization and discrimination. Cyprus is committed to building an inclusive, age-friendly society that promotes independence, support, and care. In this regard, Cyprus has adopted the first-ever national strategy and action plan for active aging. Mr. Chair, Cyprus is committed also to fostering an inclusive society founded on equality, dignity, non-discrimination and respect for all. In this context, Cyprus has taken important legislative and institutional steps to strengthen the protection of LGBTIQ+ persons and promote their rights. To that effect, the Council of Ministers approved the preparation of the first national strategy for the promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons. Cyprus has also strengthened measures and its legal framework to prevent discrimination and hate crime and hold perpetrators accountable. The protection of cultural diversity and heritage is intrinsically linked to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms and remains a priority for Cyprus. Cyprus has consistently championed the protection of cultural heritage including through the Nicosia Convention on Offences Relating to Cultural Property adopted during the chairmanship of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. The said convention is the only international treaty specifically dealing with the criminalization of the illicit trafficking of cultural property and is open for signature to all states. In this spirit, Cyprus is proud to be one of the initiators and co-chairs of the UN Group of Friends of Culture, together with Egypt, Italy, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates. Mr. Chair, in conclusion, Cyprus remains firmly committed to upholding the universality, indivisibility, and equal enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms for all. As a country that continues to endure the consequences of occupation and division, Cyprus will continue to speak for the rights of all Cypriots and to advocate for the protection of those most vulnerable. We reiterate our commitment to continuing our engagement and cooperation with all member states in the United Nations, working together to strengthen multilateralism, uphold international law, and advance a more peaceful, inclusive, and just world where human rights are respected and protected for present and future generations. I thank you.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Cyprus. I now give the floor to the representative of Greece, followed by Mexico. Representative of Greece, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. At the outset, allow me to congratulate you on your appointment and to thank you and the Bureau for guiding our work. Greece aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union and would like to add the following remarks in its national capacity. Mr. Chair, we meet at a time of profound geopolitical uncertainty, rapid technological transformation, and growing pressure on the international system. Conflicts are multiplying, humanitarian needs are rising, while new technologies including artificial intelligence, are transforming our societies at unprecedented speed. In this rapidly evolving information environment, disinformation is no longer an abstract concern. At the same time, artificial intelligence raises profound questions for human rights, human agency, and democratic values. We must therefore champion a human rights-based approach to the digital world, ensuring that technological progress serves prosperity, security, and human dignity. Against this backdrop, the principles of the United Nations Charter and the international human rights framework must remain our collective compass. International law, international humanitarian law, and international human rights law are not abstract commitments. Their consistent application is essential to international peace and security, to the protection of human dignity, and ultimately, to trust in the multilateral system. This is particularly important for small and medium-sized states. A world governed by the rule of law, rather than by power alone, is indispensable to our collective security. As the Secretary-General reminded us during the general debate, the force of law must prevail over the law of force. Greece, therefore, remains firmly committed to the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and to dialogue and diplomacy grounded in international law as a means to prevent conflict, peacefully settle disputes, and advance human rights. This commitment guides our work as an elected member of the Security Council for 2025-2026, as well as our candidature for membership of the Human Rights Council for 2028-2030. Mr. Chair, peace and security cannot be sustained without respect for human rights. This is particularly evident in the situation of children affected by armed conflict. Children continue to bear an unacceptable burden in conflicts around the world. As the designated chair of the Security Council Working Group on CAC, Greece remains firmly committed to protecting children affected by conflict and to a balanced, impartial and action-oriented implementation of the CAC mandate in close cooperation with the United Nations, UNICEF and civil society. The same commitment underpins our approach to the women, peace and security agenda. The full, equal, meaningful and safe participation of women in decision-making and peace processes is essential to sustainable peace. Guided by our National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security, Greece continues to promote the implementation of this agenda across the United Nations system. During our presidency of the Security Council this month, Greece will also convene on October 27th a high-level open debate on women, peace and security, making the anniversary of the adoption of landmark Security Council Resolution 1325. Mr. Chair, migration is another area in which the protection of human rights must remain at the center of our collective response. As a frontline European Union member state, Greece has faced sustained migratory pressures for many years. We remain committed both to the effective protection of our borders, which are also external borders of the European Union, and to full respect for international law and fundamental human rights. At the same time, an effective international response must address criminal smuggling networks, prevent the instrumentalization of migration, and support refugees, displaced persons, and host countries. Our objective must be to combine responsibility and solidarity while addressing the root causes of displacement and working towards durable solutions. Mr. Chair, allow me also to address a human rights issue of particular importance to Greece and of long-standing concern to the international community, Cyprus. For well over a half century now, since the 1974 Turkish military invasion, Turkey continues to illegally occupy 37% of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus a UN and European Union member state, in blatant violation of Article 2, paragraph 4 of the United Nations Charter and the 1960 Treaty of Guarantee, to which Turkey is a signatory party. The consequences for human rights remain profound. More than 160,000 Greek Cypriots were forced to flee their homes and properties, while acts involving the unlawful sale and exploitation of Greek Cypriot properties in the occupied areas continue to raise serious concerns. Furthermore, Cypriot cultural and religious heritage has suffered extensive and in some cases irreparable damage with more than 500 churches reportedly looted, desecrated or destroyed. The issue of missing persons remains one of the gravest consequences of the Turkish invasion of Cyprus, including for Greece as Greek citizens remain missing to this day. Moreover, the enclaved population continues to be deprived of the full enjoyment of its human rights, including property rights, religious freedom, and the right to education. We deeply regret that Turkiye has not yet taken the necessary steps to acknowledge and appropriately address the situation in Cyprus, notwithstanding numerous UN Security Council and General Assembly resolutions, as well as the pertinent judgments of the European Court of Human Rights. Greece remains unwavering in its support for a comprehensive, just, and lasting settlement of the Cyprus issue within the agreed United Nations framework on the basis of a bi-communal, bi-zonal federation with political equality as defined in the relevant Security Council resolutions with a single international personality, a single sovereignty, and a single citizenship. Mr. Chair, the challenges before this committee are diverse, but the principle that connects them is simple. Human dignity must remain at the center of our work. The Third Committee has a particular responsibility to translate the principles of the Charter and our international human rights commitments into meaningful protection for people on the ground. At a time when international cooperation is increasingly tested, our task is not to retreat from those principles, but to uphold them consistently and credibly. Greece will continue to work with all member states in that spirit, in defense of human rights, in support of international law and in the conviction that dialogue and multilateral cooperation remain indispensable to peace, security, and human dignity. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Greece. I now turn to the representative of Mexico, followed by the permanent representative of Mozambique. The representative of Mexico, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. Mexico wishes you every success together with the other members of the Bureau, and we also thank INTAM. Mexico reaffirms its commitment to the promotion and protection of all human rights and the fundamental role of this Committee so that through dialogue we can continue to promote the progressive development of international human rights law. Armed conflict, poverty, inequalities, discrimination, hate speech, and gender-based violence are becoming normalized and continue to violate the dignity and the rights of millions of people. We are facing questions over principles and norms that the international community, which had built them for decades, and with that, we are weakening the ability of multilateralism to provide our societies with effective responses. And precisely for that reason, we need to expand the spaces available for dialogue, listen another openly and build trust. The work of this committee, including informal consultations, should allow us to understand our different realities and find common ground. Every negotiation should keep in mind its end goal, which is to improve people's lives. The universality of human rights and the principles of equality and non-discrimination must guide all of our efforts. These principles, enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the main international human rights treaties, remind us that we have the duty to make sure that all people, without exception, can fully exercise their rights. This compromise requires a recognition of the interdependence of the three pillars of the United Nations, human rights, development, and peace and security. Without human rights, peace becomes illusory and development becomes an empty promise. There can be no peace where there is fear, discrimination, injustice, or forced silence. Nor can we speak of development if people are deprived of their right to education, to health, to liberty, or to equal opportunities. Without human rights, there is no justice; without justice, there is no peace; and without peace, there is no development. Therefore, we must move ahead consistently and coherently. No pillar can be consolidated in isolation. Mr. Chair, no State is free of human rights challenges. We all have the responsibility to recognize them, to address them seriously, and to be accountable over the measures taken to overcome them. Mexico is convinced that openness to international scrutiny strengthens our institutions, improves our public policies, and helps us to respond more effectively to the needs of the population. Our cooperation with the treaty bodies, the special procedures, the Universal Periodic Review and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights have allowed us to identify challenges and to work within solid and institutional frameworks. Their observations and recommendations are valuable tools for allowing our national efforts to keep moving forward. This cooperation requires sustained commitment from the States and from the mechanisms themselves. The treaty bodies also have the obligation to cooperate with States in accordance with their respective instruments and to maintain constructive dialogue. A good faith dialogue that is rigorous and results-oriented helps to strengthen national capacities and to translate international commitments into the effective protection of persons. In this spirit, Mexico, upon the invitation of the Mexican State, received the official visit of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, in April 2026. His meetings with the authorities of the various different branches of the state, civil society organizations, search collectives and public human rights bodies provided a valuable space for dialogue on the situation in the country and international challenges. This visit, together with a visit by the rapporteur for Mexico of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and other special procedures to the country, reaffirmed the value of dialogue, cooperation to strengthen international responses while centering persons, particularly victims and their families. The aim of guaranteeing all rights for all persons requires a recognition that we are not all starting from the same starting point. Historic discrimination and structural inequalities put some people and groups in a situation of greater vulnerability. Paying special attention to them allows us to identify the obstacles that prevent the universality of rights becoming a daily reality. For Mexico, the eradication of poverty is a priority in order to make the exercise of all human rights effective. Poverty and inequalities result from structural barriers and exclusions, which must and can be transformed through person-centered public policies. Mexico is promoting a model of development with wellbeing, social justice, and redistribution, which centers those people that have historically been excluded and makes the commitment to leave no one behind a reality. Between 2018 and 2024, the population in a situation of poverty in Mexico fell by 13.4 million people. In percentage terms, there was a reduction from 41.9% to 29.6% of the population, moreover, approximately 1.7 million people emerged from extreme poverty. Substantive equality and non-discrimination create the conditions to make sure that all people can access their rights and fully enjoy them. Therefore, universal policies must be supplemented with specific measures that eliminate differentiated barriers and address multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination. Mexico, in particular, reaffirms its commitment to the rights of indigenous peoples. Their full participation in the decisions that affect them is a right. The protection of their languages, cultures, territories, institutions and traditional knowledge is essential in order to build democratic societies. We will continue to promote the effective implementation of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, including their right to participate in the work of this Organization on questions that concern them. Mexico will continue to demand respect for the human rights of all migrant persons, regardless of their migration status. States must continue to work together to ensure that migrating is a free decision and not a necessity. Faced with criminalization, xenophobia, and political narratives that present migration as a threat, we must reaffirm that migrants are rights holders and must recognize their contributions to communities of origin, transit, and destination. International cooperation must be focused on expanding regular mobility routes, protecting persons in a situation of vulnerability, preventing and combating human trafficking and migrant smuggling, and to promote inclusive societies. No country can alone respond to a phenomenon that is essentially international in nature. Substantive equality will continue to be a cross-cutting pillar of Mexico's national and international action. Through our feminist foreign policy, we will continue to promote the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women in all their diversity. That involves combating the structural causes of discrimination and gender-based violence, recognizing, reducing, and redistributing non-remunerated domestic and care work, guaranteeing sexual and reproductive rights, and promoting the participation and leadership of women, teenagers and girls. That commitment also includes persons with disabilities, persons of African descent, older persons, girls, boys, teenagers, LGBTIQ+ people and all of those who are facing barriers to the full exercise of their rights. In Mexico, we embrace diversity. Our differences enrich our societies, and our shared dignity unites us. Mr. Chair, in times of polarization, this Organization needs more dialogue, more cooperation, and a renewed political will. Building trust requires listening to one another and maintaining a respectful dialogue, including when we have disagreements. It also requires acting with consistency, with principles, and avoiding selectivity, double standards, and the instrumentalization of human rights. The consensuses that we build need to be turned into results for people. We must continue moving forward without going backwards towards the full exercise of all human rights. The progress achieved must be the starting point to expand protection and close the remaining gaps. Mexico will continue to work with all States, with the United Nations system, civil society, indigenous peoples and other actors to strengthen a multilateralism that combines human rights, development and peace and security. Thank you very much.

In Mozambique, schools must keep teaching, health facilities must stay open, and vaccination and nutrition programs must continue, including in northern communities that face terrorism, displacement, and climate-related disasters at the same time. Gender equality is not only a women's agenda. It is a national development imperative essential to poverty reduction, social stability and sustainable peace. Mr. Chair, Mozambique is firmly committed to combating racial discrimination xenophobia and related intolerance and to the full implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. We attach particular importance to the dignity, equality and rights of people of African descent. For that reason, Mozambique has facilitated consultations within the United Nations on a possible update of the Programme of Activities for the implementation of the International Decade for People of African Descent. We call on all member states to carry that work through to an outcome that strengthens implementation. Our priorities encompass health, nutrition, education, child protection, water, sanitation, and hygiene, with particular attention to children living in vulnerable, remote, conflict-affected, and climate affected communities. This integrated approach is reflected in Mozambique's cooperation with the UNICEF under the country program for 2027-2030. Mozambique also remains committed to the protection of refugees and asylum seekers and continues to uphold its tradition of solidarity with those seeking protection. Our country currently hosts more than 20,000 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from other African countries. In cooperation with UNHCR and other partners, Mozambique continues to promote their access to protection and essential services while supporting self-reliance and durable solutions. I wish to thank you, the other members of the Bureau, and the Secretariat for all the work you have done and will do in the coming weeks. Please be assured that you will have Israel's full support and cooperation in the weeks ahead. Dear colleagues, yesterday, passengers and crew aboard the flight from Dubai to Israel faced a terrifying in-flight terror attack that could have ended in tragedy. The courage and quick action of the passengers and crew who helped regain control of the aircraft and enabled its safe emergency landing, saved lives, and demonstrated extraordinary bravery. This wasn't only an apparent attack against Israeli passengers, but an attempt to destroy peace and normalization. But terror will not determine the future of our region. And I think it's a needed reminder as we open this committee. I am sending my warmest wishes for a speedy recovery to the brave Indian pilot, Captain Smit Machar, who saved all those people on the plane. This is an emotionally heavy period for us. Next week will mark three years since one of the darkest moments in Israel's history. The horrific terrorist attack by Hamas on October 7, 2023, and the abduction of our people left a deep scar on our nation and on us as individuals. A trauma that will take generations to heal. Nearly a year ago, a ceasefire agreement was reached. To be frank, it is not an ideal or steady ceasefire, but it's been holding for a year and offers much needed relief to all. Unfortunately, for my family and friends back home, the attacks they have endured over the past several years have not only come from Hamas, but also from Iran, Hezbollah, and the Houthis. We face repeated attacks involving missiles and drones, forcing us to run to bomb shelters for safety, often with little warning. These attacks have affected entire families and communities, including women, children, elderly persons, and persons with disabilities, many of whom lost their lives, and many of us lost friends and family members. It is our duty, in the memory of those we lost, to ensure we move toward lasting, sustainable peace. Colleagues, as we all know in this room, words have power. With our voices and with the words we choose to use, we can make the world a better place, or we can deepen hatred, fear, and division. I know it can sometimes feel like we're negotiating inside our New York bubble, but the words we use here matter. Unfortunately, our agenda includes items whose sole purpose is to attack my country. There are powerful movements today that feed on these false narratives. and member states that benefit from spreading them. Hatred toward Israel becomes hatred toward Israelis. Hatred toward Israelis becomes hatred towards Jews. Words of hate become slogans of extremism. Slogans become actions that spread fear and ignite violence. And violence becomes terror. And so we cannot remain silent when words are weaponized here. We must recognize the consequences of what we say. challenge false narratives, and remember that the words spoken in these halls do not stay here. In the coming weeks, we will hear from many UN mandate holders who are expected to uphold the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, objectivity, impartiality, and independence in the discharge of their functions. Concerns regarding failures to meet these standards should be addressed appropriately. This is both proper and necessary. Conduct that departs from these principles risks undermining confidence in the mandate holder system, deters individuals and groups from engaging with its mechanisms, and ultimately weakens the credibility and legitimacy of the institutions and mandates they are entrusted to serve. Antisemitism is a painful example of what can happen when hateful words are normalized, allowed to be spread, and eventually turn into acts of violence. Jewish communities around the world are once again face harassment, threats, and violence. Only a few days ago, during Yom Kippur, our day of atonement, a gunman opened fire outside a synagogue in Canada in what police described as a deliberate hate-motivated attack against the Jewish community. Here, in New York, a man was charged with hate crimes after attacking a Jewish person and a security guard during Shabbat services at Central Synagogue. Unfortunately, the numbers show how far this hatred has already spread. The latest J7 report documented more than 23,000 anti-Semitic incidents across the seven largest Jewish communities outside Israel in 2025. In the United States alone, the Anti-Defamation League recorded more than 6,200 incidents last year. It's an average of 17 every day. But perhaps even more troubling is how this affects everyday life. A recent survey by Jewish Women International found that 54% of young Jewish women surveyed said they hide their Jewish identity in public in order to feel safer, while 75% reported a negative impact on their mental health. This hatred is not limited to the streets. It is also spreading online, where hateful rhetoric can reach millions of people within seconds. Antisemitism is no longer an abstract concern. For that reason, Israel launched last month the Task Force on Combating Antisemitism, bringing together UN member states that understand how dangerous it is to allow hatred to grow within our societies and that share the responsibility to protect their Jewish communities. Mr. Chair, with everything I said, Israel still believes that the Third Committee agenda is filled with resolutions that deal with some of today's most burning issues: the protection of life, advancement of rights, of women, gender equality, LGBTQI+ rights, promotion of the rights of persons with disabilities, freedom of religion or belief, and the meaningful participation of youth. We believe that the Third Committee can support meaningful changes on the ground. With this said, I want to use this platform to add a voice to our discussion. Every year, we select two exceptional future leaders who represent Israeli youth. This year, they joined us for the opening of the committee season, and we thought it will be a good use of our time to hear from one of them directly. So, Maya, please take it from here and allow us to do a quick switch, please, Mr. Chair.

Thank you, Emil. Mr. Chair, distinguished delegates, and fellow youth representative, in this hall, the international community frequently debates youth as architects of the future. But over the last three painful years, Israeli youth learned the words on paper did not protect us. Our most fundamental rights to life, to safety, to bodily integrity were shattered. I am an undergrad biology student who, like my entire generation, had to put studies, dreams, and personal milestones on hold. We were targeted at festival grounds celebrating peace and music. We saw our childhood communities devastated across the south, while many thousand endured prolonged displacement and uncertainty across northern border towns. An entire generation had to put their dreams and the innocence of young adulthood on hold. Yet, for young Israelis and Jewish worldwide, this trauma was compounded when international platforms, academic spaces, and human rights bodies met our pain with silence. And if they did speak, our grief was met with outright denial and painful skepticism. Instead of global empathy, Jewish and Israeli students increasingly faced anti-Semitic hostility, exclusion, and institutional calls for boycotts. For the same reasons, no one should feel like they have to hide who they are, their sexual orientation or gender identity, the color of their skin or ethnicity. No child should have to wonder whether it is safer to take off the kippah or whether being openly Jewish might make them a target. On social media platforms and across online spaces, our generation had witnessed how artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems can be weaponized to automate the analysis and amplify anti-Semitic hate speech. But Israel refused to be defined slowly by what was taking away from us. in Hebrew, the word for right, tsehut, shares its root with the word merit, or privilege of doing good and serving others. When international frameworks fail to shield us, we put our pain into agency. Young Israelis became the backbone of civil society, tirelessly working to heal, repair, and innovate our communities. And despite the enduring trauma, we remain fearlessly optimistic. Our optimism should not be mistaken for naivety. It is our conscious moral choice to heal and rebuild. Fulfilling the UN core principle for meaningful youth participation requires moving beyond symbolic tokenism to integrate youth as partners in recovery, reconciliation, and peace. I am proud to speak to you as the Israeli youth delegate to have the seat at the table and work towards a future where trauma gives way to healing and where all young people, Israelis and Palestinians alike, and everyone across our region entire region can finally live side by side in safety, mutual dignity, and lasting peace. Thank you very much for listening.

Preventing and responding to violence against children remains a central priority for our policies. Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine continues to have devastating consequences for children. We remain deeply concerned by the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children and call for their safe return to their families and communities. The situation of children in the Middle East also remains deeply concerning. Children in Gaza have suffered enormously as a result of the conflict that began on October 7, 2023, and the resulting humanitarian crisis. We reiterate the importance of protecting civilians, ensuring sustained and unhindered humanitarian access, and respecting international humanitarian law. The protection of children must remain central to international efforts to achieve a lasting and sustainable peace. Over the past decade, Bulgaria has made substantial progress in the institutionalization, including the closure of almost all specialized childcare institutions. Our national legal framework is based on principles of equality and non-discrimination, and we continue to strengthen the practical implementation of these principles. I thank the representatives of Bulgaria. I now pass the floor to the United States of America, followed by the permanent representative of Finland. Representative of the United States of America, you have the floor.

The United States congratulates Ambassador James Martin Larson of Australia on his chairmanship of the Third Committee for the 81st session of the General Assembly. We look forward to working closely with Australia, the Bureau, and our fellow delegations toward a productive session, one that helps return this institution to its core mission, the maintenance of international peace and security. We request that this statement be entered into the official record. Our approach to this session is straightforward and consistent with our message over the last two years. The United States seeks to bring the United Nations back to basics, anchored in three enduring pillars: peace, prosperity, and sovereignty. We will work with fellow member states to deliver concrete results, reduce bureaucratic bloat, demand accountability, and steer this committee's work away from divisive agendas and back toward its founding purpose. It is in that spirit that we hope to make this year's third committee more efficient, more relevant, and more effective. Resolutions emerging from this committee are non-binding, and they should be treated accordingly. They should be short, actionable, and forward-looking. Too many Member States return year after year to the same contentious or peripheral issues, consuming time and resources without advancing our shared mandate. The United States supports a leaner General Assembly and Third Committee, one that eliminates redundant or off-topic agenda items, reduces unnecessary meetings, and makes more strategic use of technology. The proliferation of reports, conferences, and parallel negotiating tracks does not strengthen this institution. It strains and drains it. Multilateral institutions are not ends in and of themselves. They exist to serve the interests of the sovereign nations that built them. As in the previous session, the United States will engage selectively. We will not attach our name to resolutions that recycle divisive or extraneous issues, Nor will we expend our negotiating capital on texts that drift from this institution's founding purpose and into politicized or irrelevant terrain. Where we do engage, it is because the substance aligns with clear US priorities. For instance, confronting human rights violations and abuses committed by oppressive regimes, combating trafficking in persons and drugs and crime, the protection of children, and defending religious freedom and the family. We remain ready to work with any nation that shares our determination to restore this committee to its intended purpose. The United States will also firmly oppose any effort to politicize this committee's work or erode the credibility of this institution by endlessly expanding its mandate. We reaffirm our commitment to health, to the protection of life at every stage, and to the family as the fundamental unit of society. We expect United Nations documents and programming to employ terminology that clearly and accurately refers to women and men, girls and boys. We support the elimination of discrimination on all recognized grounds, and we equally expect UN programming to avoid diversity, equity, and inclusion frameworks that come at the expense of merit, hard work, and individual achievement. The United States continues to reject the 2030 agenda and will not reaffirm it. As we open this session, the United States remains guided by a simple and consistent framework: peace, prosperity, and sovereignty. We will measure success not by the number of resolutions this committee adopts, but by whether its work meaningfully advances international peace and security and improves the lives of the people our nations serve. We hope this session marks a genuine turning point, one where member states choose efficiency over duplication, action over rhetoric, and sovereignty over politicization. The United States stands ready to work with any delegation prepared to join that effort and we look forward to building, together with Australia, the Bureau, and our fellow Member States, a third Committee that is leaner, more focused, and worthy of the trust vested in it by those who fund and depend upon it. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I thank the representative of the United States of America. I will pass the floor to the Permanent Representative of Finland, followed by Switzerland. Permanent Representative of Finland, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. And Finland, of course, aligns itself with the EU statement. Today, the world faces conflicts, instability, and human suffering at a level unseen since the founding of the United Nations. Therefore, it is now time to urgently revitalize our collective commitment to human rights and international law. Human rights are not just a pillar or a sector among other important issues. Respect for human rights is the only path towards human well-being and development and towards peaceful and truly stable societies, also in the long run. Breaches of human rights are not only wrong, they are short-sighted and will always eventually turn against those responsible. Peace, stability and sustainable development can only be reached with respect for human rights. At the UN, human rights are both foundational and instrumental in promoting the other two pillars. We need to apply human rights-based approach in development, and human rights must be at the heart of promoting peace and security globally. I want to underline that an inclusive, strong and future-oriented UN requires a renewed, uncompromising investment in human rights, both politically and in resources. Chair, there can be no lasting peace without rule of law, justice and accountability. Ending the culture of impunity requires effective legal frameworks, reliable data collection, survivor-centered investigations and judicial processes. We strongly support the work of the International Criminal Court. Shrinking civic space threatens the security, stability and well-being of entire societies. Human rights defenders are on the front lines. They continue to face harassment, torture, arbitrary arrest and detention, criminalization, executions, as well as restrictions to their freedoms of movement, expression, association and assembly. Finland condemns these actions against human rights defenders, journalists, lawyers, trade unionists, environmental defenders and others who expose violations and abuses or advocate for accountability. Media freedom is an absolute key to resilient, secure and democratic societies and stability long term. Protecting independent journalism and diverse media in the digital age is crucial. Finland is proud to co-chair the Media Freedom Coalition, advancing safety of journalists and promoting media literacy. Today, independent journalism faces existential threats. Mis- and disinformation are being deliberately weaponized to distort facts, create confusion, erode public trust and safety, and to silence critical voices. Responding to these challenges requires tools to think critically and uphold truth. The future of artificial intelligence must be guided by a human rights-based approach that preserves human agency and democratic accountability while supporting innovation and sustainable development. While AI offers significant opportunities, the technological progress must remain firmly anchored in human rights, rule of law, and meaningful human oversight. Chair, we need to ensure that gender equality and the rights of all women and girls remain at the core of our efforts. We must support intergovernmental bodies in upholding and strengthening these commitments. We must continue to empower women and girls in all their diversity and recognize that societies grow more resilient when everybody can participate fully. Universal access to comprehensive sexual and reproductive health and rights is central. Every individual must have the autonomy to make free, informed decisions over their own body and their own future. Eliminating sexual and gender-based violence is an imperative Today, women and girls continue to face violence in homes, schools, increasingly online, and in wars around the globe, from Middle East to Ukraine, Sudan, and elsewhere. We stand steadfast in solidarity with women and girls of Afghanistan. Individuals belonging to sexual and gender minorities, together with organizations defending their rights, remain among the most vulnerable groups in societies around the world. The protection and full realization of the rights and freedoms of all people, including LGBTIQ+ persons, is essential to foster trust and thriving societies. Chair, Finland is firmly committed to advancing the rights and inclusion of persons with disabilities globally. Implementation of the UN Disability Inclusion Strategy is key. Approximately 16% of the world's population live with a disability. They are not a small minority. These are people whose talent and contributions are vital to building resilient and prosperous societies. Yet too many still face barriers to education, employment, participation, and access to services. As ongoing conflicts tragically increase the number of people living with disabilities, inclusive action becomes even more urgent. When we advance disability inclusion, we strengthen our societies as a whole and ensure that no one is left behind. Chair, Finland voices her continued commitment to the fulfilment of the rights of indigenous peoples, both nationally and globally. We must take concrete steps forward in the enhanced participation process, and we welcome the adoption of the recent GA resolution in this regard. We must provide indigenous peoples, through representatives chosen by themselves, full and effective participation in the UN in matters that concern their rights. Chair, we must defend the human rights of all people in all spheres of life with a steadfast focus on equality and non-discrimination of those in the most vulnerable situations. Lasting peace and sustainable development cannot be achieved in isolation. It requires meaningful participation and dialogue and the active and inclusive participation of all parts of the societies. Thank you, and I will now pass the floor to our youth delegate.

Thank you. Before coming to New York, I brought young people together at the Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs to discuss AI, technology, and human rights. And one message was clear. Young people welcome technological progress, but we want human rights, responsibility, and education to keep pace with it. AI is developing fast, and the choices we make today shape our societies and future generations. and technological development must uphold human rights from the beginning. Women and girls face violence, harassment and hate speech online. AI can make harmful content easier to create and spread. Women and girls must be protected in digital spaces and they must also be

represented in the development of new technologies.

We need clear rules, but regulation alone is not enough. Skills to understand technology, question information, and make informed decisions are becoming even more important. Technology can be a powerful tool. We should shape technological development rather than let it shape our societies for us. I encourage the international community to keep human rights at the center of technological development. By doing so, we can build a digital future based on human rights, trust and peace.

Thank you. I thank the permanent representative of Finland and the youth delegate of Finland. And I will pass to Switzerland before then passing to the permanent representative of Iceland. Switzerland, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. Chair, this year we are celebrating two major milestones for the international human rights system. On the one hand, it is the 60th anniversary of the two international covenants on human rights. These landmark conventions continue to embody a fundamental principle: civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights are universal, indivisible and interdependent. On the other hand, This year marks the 20th anniversary of the establishment of the Human Rights Council. Over the past two decades, the Council has become a central pillar of the international human rights architecture and a forum for dialogue, helping to strengthen effective implementation and advance international standards. In every region of the world, conflicts, discrimination and inequalities continue to affect people. Civic space is shrinking. violations persist, and new technologies are creating new challenges for human rights. As we mark this year the 75th anniversary of the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, the number of forcibly displaced people remains at an all-time high. In this context, it is incumbent upon Member States to ensure that the principles enshrined 60 years ago continue to guide our actions today. Chair, for Switzerland, human rights are not merely a guiding principle. They constitute legal obligations that states have freely accepted. They are inseparable from the stability of international order, from security, from peace and sustainable development. In a changing multilateral environment, this also requires us to adapt our approach. Switzerland is committed to effective and coherent multilateralism. in which international organizations complement and reinforce each other. In the field of human rights, we believe that priority should be given to impact and to strengthening the implementation of existing frameworks. As a member of the Human Rights Council for the period 2025-2027, Switzerland intends to contribute actively to this. Our new guidelines on human rights for 2026-2029 also place implementation, coherence and concrete impact at the heart of our human rights diplomacy. This ambition is all the more important given that the UN system is under significant financial and political pressure. The human rights pillar remains structurally underfunded in relation to the scope of the mandates entrusted to it. As part of the UN80 reform, Switzerland advocates for a balanced approach to the three pillars of the United Nations. Investing in human rights also means investing in conflict prevention, stability and lasting peace. It's in this spirit that we are committed to strengthening the treaty bodies. Last June, we brought together in Switzerland representatives of states from all regions, chairpersons of treaty bodies, Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and civil society, with a view to giving fresh impetus to pragmatic reforms of existing mandates. These reforms aim in particular to ensure a more efficient and predictable reporting process as well as a better follow-up for the benefit of rights holders. We invite the treaty bodies and the Office of the High Commissioner to intensify their ownership of this strengthening process. This would also require sustained political and financial commitment from member states. Reforms and adequate resources go hand in hand. Strengthening the system also depends on preserving the ecosystem that sustains it. In this regard, Geneva offers a safe and inclusive environment, unique in its expertise in dialogue and cooperation. Switzerland will also continue to support the Office of the High Commissioner and, as the host state, it will continue to safeguard the conditions enabling all stakeholders to contribute to international human rights work, free from intimidation or reprisals. Finally, Switzerland recognizes the close link between human rights, democracy, peace and security. Their promotion and protection form an integral part of a comprehensive, cooperative and rules-based approach to security. This approach is also reflected in the priorities of the Swiss chairmanship of the OSCE regarding democracy, the rule of law and human rights. Chair, I would now like to highlight three priorities for Switzerland for this session of the Third Committee. Firstly, Switzerland will continue to work towards a moratorium on the use of the death penalty, with a view to its universal abolition. Today, with Mexico and on behalf of a group of 45 States, we will present the 11th resolution on this issue. Today, 77% of States have abolished the death penalty or have introduced a moratorium. We note with the deepest concern that in 2025, 17 countries still carried out executions and the number of recorded executions rose by around 80% compared to 2024. Switzerland encourages all Member States to support this resolution. There can be no justice that kills. Secondly, we will promote and defend fundamental freedoms, which includes safeguarding civic space. Switzerland is particularly concerned about restrictions targeting human rights defenders, journalists and civil society. At the same time, we must combat discrimination, hate speech and incitement to violence, including online, while safeguarding freedom of expression and freedom of religion or belief. In this regard, Switzerland is working with the Office of the High Commissioner and the organization Article 19 to promote the effective implementation of the Rabat Action Plan in the digital environment. Practical recommendations will be presented on the sidelines of this session at an event in late October. Thirdly, we will continue to defend women's rights and gender equality. In the face of growing resistance to the rights of women and girls, Switzerland is committed to safeguarding the achievements made and the existing international framework, particularly in relation to gender-based violence and discrimination. It also reaffirms its commitment to non-discrimination. particularly against LGBTIQ people, as illustrated by its first national action plan against hate crimes targeting them, adopted this year. Chair, I'd like to conclude by reiterating that it is precisely in times of adversity that human rights are put to the test. It is then that we see whether they are truly respected for everyone, but without discrimination. Promoting and protecting them is a collective responsibility that rests with us at all times. 60 years ago, the covenants affirm that all human rights are universal, indivisible and interdependent. 20 years ago, we established a council to bring them to life. Let us live up to this legacy by preserving a universal, credible and effective human rights system. that is capable of responding to today's challenges. Switzerland will continue to contribute to this alongside its partners and in a spirit of cooperation. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Switzerland and I pass the floor to the Permanent Representative of Iceland, to be followed by the Permanent Representative of Montenegro. Iceland, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr Chair. Let me begin by congratulating you, Ambassador Larsen, and the rest of the Bureau on your election. We would like to express our sincere appreciation for your work so far and wish you all the best in guiding the Committee through this 81st session. Mr. Chair, we are witnessing a deeply troubling global backlash against fundamental human rights. Persistent challenges continue to impact the human rights landscape with a continued rise in conflicts, democratic backsliding, and shrinking of civic space, negatively impacting the realization of human rights globally. Armed conflicts rage across the world, resulting in widespread human rights violations and severe humanitarian crisis, often escalated by restrictions on humanitarian access and attacks against humanitarian personnel. The digital transformation is reshaping our societies and civic space. The same technologies that empower can also be used to monitor, silence or manipulate. Recognizing this is essential, as is taking action to ensure that digital technologies strengthen democratic participation and human rights. Climate change continues to threaten the effective enjoyment of a range of human rights, including those to life, water and sanitation, food, health, housing and self-determination. The reintroduction of the death penalty by some States is of grave concern and must be viewed as a step backwards for human rights. Ongoing use of capital punishment as a tool for intimidation and control can never be justified. These concerning trends underscore the importance of renewed multilateral action. This is not happening in isolation. It is a part of a wider erosion of democratic values and the rules-based international order. For a small state like Iceland, whose security and prosperity depends on these values, this is not an abstract concern. It's existential. Human rights are at the core of Iceland's foreign policy, and they must remain at the heart of our collective efforts. Mr Chair, As a member of the Human Rights Council through 2027, Iceland places particular emphasis on gender equality, LGBTQI+ rights, and the rights of children and young persons. The pushback against gender equality and the rights of women and girls is increasingly more organized, with many countries reshaping laws to restrict freedoms and silence voices. Women and girls continue to face structural inequalities and multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination. Sexual and gender-based violence, exploitation, abuse and harassment are worldwide problems which we must address urgently on all levels. Iceland remains steadfast in its commitment to advancing the human rights of women and girls in all their diversity, with a special focus on working collaboratively towards zero tolerance for sexual and gender-based violence and promoting universal access to sexual and reproductive health and rights. Eradicating disparity between genders is not only the right thing to do, but it also increases the prosperity and well-being of societies. Mr. Chair, too many persons of diverse sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics continue to face discrimination and violence solely for being who they are. Iceland remains concerned about alarming crackdowns on civil society organizations and arrests of persons fighting for the recognition of these basic human rights. These are not isolated incidents. They are part of a broader pattern threatening people's dignity, equality, and safety. No person should have to live in fear of persecution and violence. Discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity is unacceptable. Human rights are not a zero-sum game, and allowing a LGBTQI+ person to live freely does not make anyone else live less free. Iceland will continue to protect the human rights of LGBTQI+ persons and advocate for the advancement of their rights worldwide. Mr Chair, Iceland firmly believes that the right of children should be placed at the centre of all policy-making. Every child has the right to grow and prosper to adulthood in good health and education, dignity and peace. We must support and enable girls and young women, in all their diversity, to prosper. Ensuring equal access to education is imperative in this regard. This includes providing young people with sexual and reproductive health rights and services, comprehensive sexuality education, and protecting the right to bodily autonomy, privacy, and self-determination. We must also continue to fight child sexual exploitation and abuse, as as well as harmful practices, including female genital mutilation and child, early and forced marriage. Mr Chair, Iceland condemns in the strongest terms Russia's ongoing illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. We condemn the targeting of civilians and critical infrastructure, such as energy facilities and heating systems, with devastating effects on all aspects of life. We further condemn the unlawful, large-scale deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children, which may amount to crimes against humanity. Russia's grave violation of international human rights and humanitarian law must end. In Russia, the systematic erosion of human rights and continued crackdown on civil society is of serious concern. We urge Russia to cease its violations of freedom of opinion and expression, and its dismantling of all forms of independent civic activity and political opposition. Palestinians continue to face appalling conditions, particularly in Gaza, where basic needs are far from being met. The situation in the West Bank is deteriorating, with unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansions undermining the possibility of a just and lasting peace. Iceland reiterates its strong support for the Palestinian people's right to self-determination and to the implementation of the two-state solution. Mr Chair, the human rights situation in the Islamic Republic of Iran continues to decline and is further intensified by the ongoing conflict. Iceland is deeply concerned by the escalation in the use of lethal force and mass arrests to suppress protests, as well as the sharp rise in executions and the use of the death penalty as a tool of intimidation and control. We call on the Islamic Republic of Iran to immediately end the use of the death penalty, impose a moratorium on executions, and release all persons arbitrarily detained. We further call on all parties to the conflict to respect international humanitarian law and human rights law. In Afghanistan, the Taliban's institutionalized and systematic repression of women and girls is intensifying. Afghan women face severe restrictions based on new decrees that further institutionalize discrimination in all aspects of life. Iceland supports Afghan women in calling for the codification of the crime of gender apartheid in international law and calls on the de facto authorities to fulfill Afghanistan's international human rights obligations and reverse policies and addictions that violate them. The situation in Sudan remains catastrophic. The relentless war continues to cause mass displacement and widespread civilian suffering, where reports of systematic sexual violence are of particular concern. Urgent protection and accountability is vital. Mr. Chair, Iceland is deeply committed to the future sustainability of the human rights treaty body system. We must join efforts to fully implement resolution 68/268 on strengthening the system. To this end, Iceland will be presenting its biannual resolution during this session. We depend on your support so it can be adopted without a vote, as it has been for the past 10 years. Mr. Chair, as a member of the Human Rights Council, Iceland has prioritized constructive engagement, open dialogue, and close cooperation with civil society organizations and human rights defenders. We firmly believe that human rights are universal, indivisible, and interdependent. We will continue to advocate for multilateral cooperation and upholding the principles of human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. Our organization is built on three pillars: human rights, development, and peace and security. One cannot thrive and prosper without the others. The promotion of human rights for everyone, everywhere, at all times is not simply a moral imperative; it is a strategic necessity fundamental to upholding our international system. Let us work together to defend these rights in our work through this Committee and beyond. I thank you.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Iceland. I invite the Permanent Representative of Montenegro to take the floor, followed by the representative of the United Kingdom. Montenegro, you have the floor.

Mr. Chair, Montenegro attaches particular importance to the work of the Third Committee. This year, our responsibility is further strengthened by our service to the Bureau of the 3C. We approach this role with a strong commitment to constructive dialogue, transparency, and consensus building, and with full respect for the views of all member states. Colleagues, the challenges before us could hardly be more pressing. In Ukraine, civilians, particularly children, continue to bear the unacceptable human cost of Russia's war of aggression. Montenegro reiterates the need for full respect for international humanitarian law and international human rights law and for accountability for violations. As a member of the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, Montenegro continues to call for the safe return of all children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred. We remain committed to a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace firmly grounded in the UN Charter and international law. In Gaza, Civilians must be protected and humanitarian assistance must reach those in need safely and without obstruction. Montenegro supports a negotiated two-state solution with Israel and an independent and viable Palestinian state living side by side in peace, security, and mutual recognition. Different conflicts have different histories, but human dignity cannot be subject to different standards. We must equally resist allowing crises outside global spotlight, including Sudan, Myanmar and Haiti, to become forgotten. Montenegro will continue to support international efforts aimed at protecting civilians, ensuring humanitarian access and advancing accountability. We are deeply concerned about the systematic restrictions imposed on women and girls in Afghanistan. Their rights to education, work, and participation in public life are fundamental human rights. No society can achieve sustainable development while excluding half of its population. excellencies. The principles we advocate internationally must also guide our action at home. This year, Montenegro adopted its Foreign Policy Strategy 2026-29, setting out a clear vision of Montenegro as a reliable and responsible international partner, guided by democratic values and respect for human dignity. The strategy places particular emphasis on the promotion of human rights and freedoms, gender equality and inclusion. As a future EU member, these priorities are reflected across our engagement at bilateral and multilateral level. In 2026, we adopted a new law on gender equality, further strengthening gender mainstreaming across public administration, including gender responsive policymaking, budgeting and data collection. For Montenegro, gender equality is not simply a sectoral issue. It is a matter of human rights and democratic governance. We continue to prioritize full, equal and meaningful participation of all women and girls in political, economic and public life, as well as combating gender-based violence and all forms of discrimination. In another important milestone for women's rights and health, Montenegro introduced paid menstrual leave for women with secondary dysmenorrhea, one of the few in Europe to do so. We also remain committed to advancing WPS agenda, recognizing the full participation of women is essential to conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and lasting peace. Montenegro attaches equal importance to the rights of children. We continue to advance the transition from institutional care towards family and community-based services. Our objective is clear. Institutional placement should remain a measure of last resort for the shortest appropriate period and always guided by the best interest of the child. Important progress has already been achieved. Today, there are no children under the age of three in residential care in Montenegro, while the overall share of children in residential care has significantly been reduced over the past decade. At the same time, we continue to strengthen foster care, family support services, and early prevention of family separation. Our strategy on deinstitutionalization for 2025-28, together with the relevant social and child protection strategies, provides framework for further transition towards community-based care. We are also working towards establishing barnhouse model in Montenegro, bringing relevant services together in child-friendly environment for children who are victims or witnesses of violence. Montenegro also remains firmly committed to advancing the rights and full participation of persons with disabilities. Dedicated parliamentary session and inclusion of persons with disabilities in the work of the Parliament have helped bring their voices closer to decision makers and strengthen their participation in democratic processes. We continue to advance independent living, accessibility, inclusive education and community-based support while removing barriers to their full and equal participation in society. Montenegro also recognizes young people not only as beneficiaries of our policies, but as partners in shaping them, and remains committed to strengthening their meaningful participation in decision-making at all levels. At the same time, we remain committed to the rights and inclusion of older persons, minorities and LGBTI persons, and to combating racism, xenophobia, hate speech and all other forms of discrimination. As a multi-ethnic, multi-religious and multicultural society, we know that diversity is not a challenge to be managed, but a strength to be protected. These are the lowest levels seen in the history of our country. It is an important milestone, but we know that a lot still needs to be done. Our priority is now to keep creating conditions so that more Paraguayans can make progress based on their own efforts and to ensure that those who are in the greatest vulnerability have the support that they need. The Zero Hunger in Schools program today ensures that more than a million pupils in 263 districts in the country have food. In addition to improving the school feeding of our children, it also helps make sure that they stay in school and generates important momentum in local economies. Through a program named after Wagadani word, our second language, this program supports vulnerable families. There is also a universal pension for older adults, which reaches more than 300,000 people. Around 450,000 housing solutions have been provided across the country, primarily for families that need that support. The aim of those policies is not only to provide assistance; we also want to create conditions to ensure that people have more opportunities, better autonomy and better opportunities to get ahead. Similarly, this same criteria guides our work with persons with disabilities. During the same period, the National Office provided services to many users and more than 14,000 people gained access to social protection services and job opportunities, education and housing opportunities. Between July 2025 and April 2026, more than 17,000 women gained access to production credits for micro-entrepreneurship, and more than 1,500 received care in specialised prevention, care and protection services. Paraguay has been strengthening early childhood work and strengthening activities to prevent violence, abuse, exploitation and child labour. We are making progress on the implementation of 50 comprehensive early child care centers. At the same time, the Abiratho Embrace program in the recent period reached more than 3,700 boys, girls, and teenagers. Young people also face a challenge in terms of creating opportunities for them through government fellowships. And that is on top of initiatives such as Connected Youth, which aims to strengthen capacities which are today needed in order to access employment and jobs, above all, decent jobs. I also wish to mention, Chair, indigenous peoples. They are an essential part of the identity and cultural diversity of Paraguay. Our country continues to work to guarantee their rights, to improve their living conditions, and to facilitate access to basic services and opportunities, while always respecting their cultures, their languages, and their traditions. In the most recent period, more than 400 indigenous families gained access to legal land rights of their territories, and 83 communities benefited from water access and community infrastructure projects. Another subject of concern to us, in particular, is the global drug problem. Paraguay believes it is necessary to maintain a balanced approach, working on prevention, treatment and rehabilitation, and at the same time firmly combating illicit smuggling and organised crime. For a country such as ours, this is a question that requires international cooperation and, above all, shared responsibility. International cooperation must support and strengthen those efforts. They are first and foremost measured by what happens in people's daily lives. For that reason, Paraguay will continue to participate intensively in the work of this committee with an openness to dialogue, defending its principles and pursuing consensus that will allow us to all move forward. Thank you very much.

The fundamental rights enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights have not changed. What has evolved is our understanding of their scope and effective protection. Over eight decades, we have deepened our understanding of the independence of civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights, and have recognized that human rights are universal because every person, without distinction, is entitled to dignity, equality, and freedom. For the Republic of Moldova, human rights are not merely abstract principles. but enduring values protected not by declaration alone, but by institutions and function, laws that are respected, and societies in which people can exercise their rights without fear. Moldova's approach is centered on free, mutual, and enforcing elements, strong institutions, meaningful participation, and accountability in an increasingly complex security and information environment.
